idiom_name: (T, error) multiple return values with errors.Is / errors.As for the reason
implementation_notes: Go's multiple return values put both outcomes in the signature: the value plus an error interface that carries the reason, so the classic Either type is unnecessary - `if err != nil` is the branch and an early return is the short-circuit. Sentinel errors created with errors.New, wrapping with fmt.Errorf("%w") and the errors.Is/errors.As helpers give the case discrimination that other languages get from an enum, and a custom error struct exposes extra fields to callers. Rebuild the structure only when an outcome has to be stored in a collection or serialized - a small generic pair inside your package - and convert back to (T, error) at the API edge, because Go callers expect the tuple.
pitfalls: The value returned alongside a non-nil error is unspecified (normally the zero value): never read it before checking the error, and never model 'no result' with a zero value that is also a legal result.
%w exposes the wrapped error to callers through errors.Is/errors.As, so wrapping is an API decision: keep the wrapped error's type stable or callers that unwrap break silently.

errors.As needs a pointer to a variable of the target error type, and a custom error type must implement Error() on the value or the pointer consistently - mixing the two makes both the assertion and errors.As fail.
A hand-written Either[T, E] fights the idiom: no exhaustive switch, no ? operator, and every caller has to learn the new shape - keep it package-private if you need one at all.
